summary: A Medium tutorial by Dinesh Kumar K B, published in Geek Culture on Sep 12, 2022, showing how to dockerize a minimalistic Flask application. It walks through a simple my_flask.py app with a /hello endpoint, a requirements.txt pinning flask==2.2.2, a Dockerfile based on python:3.9-slim-buster, building and running the image as myflaskapp, and pushing it to Docker Hub.
one_line: Tutorial on containerizing a minimal Flask app with a Dockerfile, building and running the image, and pushing it to Docker Hub.
key_facts: The tutorial's objective is to dockerise a minimalistic Flask application.
The example Flask app has a single endpoint /hello and the module is named my_flask.py.
The /hello endpoint returns jsonify({"msg": "Hello from Flask"}).
The requirements.txt file for the example contains flask==2.2.2.
The Dockerfile uses FROM python:3.9-slim-buster as its base image.
The Dockerfile sets WORKDIR /app, exposes port 5000, and sets ENV FLASK_APP=my_flask.py.
The Dockerfile CMD is ["flask", "run", "--host", "0.0.0.0"] so the server accepts requests from all hosts.
The image is built with the command docker build -t myflaskapp . and the trailing period is required.
After building, the myflaskapp:latest image is listed at 133MB in docker images.
The image is run with docker run -p 5000:5000 myflaskapp.

The article quotes Docker's definition: a container is a standard unit of software that packages up code and all its dependencies so the application runs quickly and reliably from one computing environment to another.
Docker Hub is described as a hosted repository service provided by Docker for finding and sharing container images with your team.
Images are pushed to Docker Hub with the docker push command in the form docker push <username>/<reponame>:tagname.
The article notes that most organisations use JFrog artifactory to host internal Docker images.
The author is Dinesh Kumar K B, a Python Back-End Developer and CKAD holder, and the post is tagged Python, Flask, Docker, Dockerfiles and Dockerize.
